div.head: LIVERPOOL WATER BILL.
div.p: LIVERPOOL WATER BILL.

SPECIAL REPORT OF THE SELECT COMMITIRE. onTtre Liverpool Wooer Bth, . peteented to the lt,coee of Commons It, accordance with their instruction, the committee have inquired into the present and prospective sufficiency of the water supply of the district which the 'Corporation of Liverpool are authorised to 'imply. They have received evidence which soti.ties them that the need for an additional supply ie extremely urgent, and that the I lather available nources m to which they have also taken evidence are open to various objections, from which the etherne proposed by the hill is comparatively free. In particular there aeems to be mfficient reintone why the Coe- . ['oration of Liverpool should have preferred the echerne . submitted to any project for takirl4 Water front the Cumber- : Lend lakes, whether iu cmnection with the Manchester aqueduct front Thirlmere, or whether from come other of those lakes. They ace also winded that the various interest, affected by the scheme in the Severn Valley have . been sufficiently guarded, and that the pressure exercised by the petitionerr ageing the bill has resulted in such modifi- cation. as will render its effect salutary rather than the reverse to for an their imeresm are concerned as regarde the tishiug, tuvigation, and the effect of boob. The corn- , mittee hove oleo inquired further, and are satisfied that the abstraction of water from the Severn Valley, an contern- plated by the scheme, is not eo great an amount as to inter- fere seriously with any plan which may hereafter to found expedient for the water supply of the town population in the Severn Valley, or even in the metropolis. In conclusion, the committee have considered the precedent furniehed in the case of the Manchester Water Act, into which a clauae was inserted by the committee on the bill, giving certain rights and facilities to the popolation on the line of the aqueduct between Thirlinere and Manchester. The mmmit- , tee have not considered it expedient that this precedent should be literally followed in the prment case. There seems to be no e.t.a for the insertion of such • provision in reepect of the diatrict Which lies between the source, of the Verniew and the Mersey ; but with regard to the populous and important direr'. in Lan.iehire lying north of the Mersey, viz., Warrington, Widnes. and St. Helens, they have required and secured that cellato facilitim for future water soupy shad be affwded by the corporation of Liverpool under' agreements. It does not seem expedient in the present case to carry obligations of this kind further, so rie to fain& the watershed of the Severn In le unduly drained north- wards, but suleMntially the Manchester precedeol has to this extent been recognised and followed. The attention of the committee having been drawn le eeveral points of impor- tance by the report of the Local Government Board, they have made several amendments in the clauses accordingly, and have reduced the period of 100 years I within yehich it was proposed akat the borrowed money ehnuld be repaid} to the shorier period of 70 years, allowing. however, ten year, to elmpe, from the passing of the net before the commence- meut of the operetion of the sinking fund:' A draft special report, as follows, woe proposed by Sir JOHN LIWIXICW:—" I regret that I one unable to concur in the report proposed by the chairman. love, indeed, utis- . lied that Liverpool is acting wisely in selecting power to ! extend her water eupply, and (do not deny that the objec- time originally entertained by the Severn Commiseionem have been fully and satisfactorily met. The population of Ike country is, however. rapidly increasiog. and the time I may come when it will be necemary to utilise all the avail- able water supply. The principal eources are the Cumber. land and Westmoreland lakes, awl the mountainous district of Wales. It is obviously natural Hut our northern cities should derive their supplies of water from the northern lakes, leaving the southern area for the rapidly growing population in the midland and southern mantles. It is not disputed that the Cumberland and Westmoreland lakes contain a supply of water abundantly sufficient,andof at least equal quality to that now proposed. The Duke of I Richmond's commission, which sat in Ms, unanimously reported that the northern lobes were • the 1..4 source of !apply for large and grow Mg mamas of population in the north and centre of England,' and laid it down se beiug sermg in principle th.at any one town or district should rake possession of the gathering ground geographically belonging to another. 'lt appears to us,' they continued. `that the Legislature Amid always jealously watch any proposal for a town taking wafer front a gathering ground at a distance from it, lest by so doing it may deprive other places nearer to such gathering ground of their more natural I course of supply ;' a principle which, moreover, wee unani-1 mously adopted by the Committee of this house on the Man- chester Corporation Water Bill which sat in 1070. The eouthern cities, and eepecially the metropolis, had no locus Korai, and no opportunity of beiag heard before the committee. Under theae circumstances, and though I have a profound reepect for the very eminent authori- ties who were called on behalf of the Liverpool cor- poration, and who gave very clear and definite evidence, I couleur that I think that before permitting Liverpool to take a supply of water so for out of her nawral area, Parliament ought to have sime independent evidence on three points— (l) As to the difficulty of obtaining a supply from the northern lakes, and (2) from the sour,es of the Dee and, likewise (3) how for the proposed scheme, either by occupy- ing an ees,mtial portion of Ott gathering ground or a district which is epecially Adapted for the construction of reservoir, would prevent 'Bristol, Birmingham, and other midland cities. or the metropolis, from hereafter obtaining a sufficient supply of water from the Welsh mountains." . . . . . _ .

Oa the queetton befog put that Sir J. Lubbock report should be sulntituted for that of the clmirman, the voting was—Ayes, Sir John Lubbock, Mr. Blennorha.cett an.. Mr. Joneph Pease, Mr. Ewart, Mr. Mlanran. The chairman's report was then adopted, and became the spacial draft report of the select committee.

The occasion was the preventing to Mr. Joseph Brunt of a silver goblet by the tern, as a token of their appreciation of his fifty rears' . faithful services. Mr. Ernest V. Bibby made the pre- sentation, and spoke eulogistically of Mr. Brunta services during the last fifty years he had been amongst them. On Saturday. about 170 of the workpeople went by the 600 train to Garston, thence by boat to Llandudno. A number of special carriages were attached to the ordinary train. Mr. Edwin H. Mows son of the station master, conducted the party. Garston was left at ten minutes to nine, and Llan- dudno reached at ten minutes past eleven. The party broke up ioto groups and visited the various points of interest to be met with. Half an hour was spent in Conway village, and considerable attention was paid to the castle. the eacor- eionista--aa escuraionists are wont to do—engraving their names no the woodtvork to Is found in the castle. Varinum relics in the castle of the "good old times," having been well surveyed, the party returned to Llandudno. Some went in runoff boats on the nee, and others drove round Great Ormea Head, and viewed the delightful scenery to be frond in the district. A band of music accompanied the excursionist, and rendered mnsl service, considering that the weather before norm was anything hut favourable. On the return journey cheers were given for Mr. Bibby and Mr. McGregor, the manager, and the train snivel at St. Helena, at 10.35.
